31: The camp holds twelve pilgrims and two pack goats. Their leader, Mer, can promise labor but cannot transfer the stone to either shrine without a council vote. The neighboring keeper, Asa, is authorized to offer water access for one day at a time. The landslide happened yesterday; its cause is not in dispute, but no one has measured how long the new stream course will last. The upstream track takes half a day in dry weather. Rain is forecast but has not begun. Mer believes the investigation would delay reaching the stone; that is an estimate, not a measured travel schedule. The next scene is a meeting at the spring, before anyone leaves camp. Whether the stone has any healing power remains an open question.
32: Rumi manages serving order and the hot-water trolley. Delegate Senn can introduce her but cannot certify language expertise. The visiting group consists of three people who exchange places at the table after each course; no rank has been established from that behavior. The interpreter's expected arrival is after the second course, although the transport desk has not confirmed a time. The broken dishwasher is behind a closed kitchen door and cannot be heard from the dining room. Rumi has heard it daily for six months. Her imitation uses taps on a spoon rather than words. The delegation's first briefing described all repeated clicks as greetings, but it offered no recordings or translations. That briefing is a hypothesis and should remain attributed. The next scene covers the first course only.
33: Growers Enna and Vo each employ one seasonal worker. The lease predates the stream's move and contains no procedure for redrawing the property map. Both growers signed it and both accept that the ladder is shared property. Enna keeps it overnight because her shed is dry; that storage arrangement does not give her sole ownership. Frost is expected in two days. Vo estimates that pruning will take one morning per orchard, but neither worker has checked the northern rows. Enna prefers not to cross alone after an earlier argument. Vo has offered to carry the ladder together, an offer not yet accepted. The next scene should concern access and work scheduling, not a magical cure for the frost or a final legal boundary ruling.
34: The former prisoner's name is Emil; the officer is Lotte. They have exchanged one letter since the war, limited to arranging the medal's return. Emil knows Lotte sheltered him for three nights and that she later disclosed his route. He does not know whether anyone threatened her. Lotte has made no explanation, and the source does not establish one. The memorial organizers want names for a public roll, not a private seating list. Two survivors asked Emil not to identify them. Lotte has no permission from either survivor. The medal belongs to her; returning it transfers no other obligation. The next scene begins at her doorstep and may end with an agreement to write to the organizers. It need not settle forgiveness or reveal the other survivors' identities.
35: The apprentice, Soli, is paid weekly and has already bought supplies for the wedding cake. Hana controls that wage account; Lio controls the delivery van booking. The van must be returned at six. Their customer has approved the cake design, so design changes cannot solve the scheduling conflict without a new conversation. The shop can operate with either baker present, but the glaze needs two people for a brief lift. They have promised the apprentice an uninterrupted lunch break. Lio interprets Hana's refusal as reluctance about the date; Hana has only spoken about wages. Neither interpretation has been tested in conversation. The next scene occurs while the glaze cools, before the four o'clock delivery. A workable compromise is possible, but none is yet canon.
36: The uncredited designer is Min Ader, employed for five weeks as a valve drafter. Zed can read the payroll dates and payment amounts, but the ledger contains no technical drawings. The prototype in the tram depot has a later replacement valve, so inspecting it cannot directly establish the original design. Museum curator Bera controls the plaque wording and has asked for evidence before making a change. The mayor is not known to have seen the ledger. A retired machinist remembers Min working late; the memory is uncorroborated and supplies no invention date. The next scene is Zed's conversation with Bera at the depot. It may establish a reason to investigate or change how the jubilee describes the work, but it cannot award sole inventorship from these materials.
37: Deputies Ora and Ben each have authority to schedule volunteers but neither can certify the gate. Technician Hadi can test its manual release; the motor requires a part due tomorrow. The siren itself passed yesterday's sound check. The public drill can rehearse gathering points without opening the gate, though the printed announcement currently promises a full demonstration. Only the chair can sign a permanent amendment, while any deputy may issue a temporary postponement with a written reason. These are separate powers. Ora suspects the chair left to avoid responsibility, but no evidence supports that explanation. Ben last saw the chair at the supply shed yesterday. The next scene should resolve what the deputies tell the waiting public, leaving both the gate's safety and the chair's whereabouts uncertain.
38: Sol learned the paper-folding method from a sibling. The boats travel over a marked ten-step distance, so their relative arrival times compare surface currents at the same moment. Wind may affect them; none of the measurements gives a load rating. Caravan leader Dea controls departure and can authorize waiting until tomorrow. The engineer is expected that evening, without a confirmed return time. One plank near the bank is visibly split. The center supports cannot be seen from shore. A narrow upstream path exists on an old map, but nobody in the group has surveyed it this season. Sol proposes sending a walker to inspect that route while they wait; Dea has not answered. The next scene should distinguish useful observation, structural uncertainty, and decisions still needing consent.
